public_rationale: The April benchmark snapshot supports the ordinary distinction Marcus draws. The same agent configuration passed functional checks on 84.4% of tasks but security checks on only 7.8%. That is substantial working-code capability with much weaker security assurance. Earlier research also reports deterioration under repeated extension, while other research shows that external diagnostic feedback can improve generated code. The evidence supports a practical robustness gap, not an impossibility claim or a causal verdict about next-word prediction.
limitations: The benchmark uses tasks derived from known vulnerabilities, so its percentages must not be generalized to all generated code.
Endor Labs sells security products; the decisive source is its own research announcement.
Security is one component of robustness, and passing security tests does not prove the absence of vulnerabilities.
The April date identifies the published capability snapshot rather than the execution dates of its underlying trials.

our_interpretation: The plain reading is that contemporary LLM coding systems can produce substantial working code while offering weaker assurance of security, reliability, and maintainability.
'Surprisingly' expresses an attitude rather than a numerical threshold.

Treat 'next-word prediction' as shorthand for the LLM coding systems discussed in the post, including their deployed agent workflows. This does not establish that a training objective causes the observed weaknesses.
For the ongoing state described on May 1, use April 2026, the latest complete calendar month, and assess the publicly reported capability snapshot during that month.
A substantial functional-versus-security gap across tested systems can support the ordinary claim without establishing failure in every dimension of robustness or every deployment.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous evaluations show substantial success at producing working code alongside materially lower success on additional security, reliability, or maintainability checks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative contemporaneous evaluations show that successful code generation generally carries comparable assurance of security, reliability, and maintainability, with no material additional gap.

evidence.explanation: The April 15 published benchmark snapshot reports 84.4% functional correctness and 7.8% security correctness for Cursor with Claude Opus 4.6. These paired results support a substantial gap; the event date denotes the reported snapshot, not the dates individual benchmark runs were executed.

This earlier study examines repeated extensions of agent-generated code and reports deterioration in structural quality. It broadens the context beyond security, but its March findings are not treated as an April outcome.

The study reports weak self-detection of correctness and safety problems, but also substantial ability to repair flawed code when supplied with test or analysis feedback. That favorable finding limits any stronger interpretation that LLM systems cannot help improve robustness.
